title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the summer we used to have

questions.prompt: In which of these sentences can "would" replace "used to" without breaking the sentence?

options.text: We used to walk to the lighthouse after dinner.
Nabil used to be afraid of the open sea.
Mona used to hate long car journeys.
The village boys used to swim across the bay in August.

questions.explanation: "Would" + base form replaces "used to" only when the verb names an action repeated in the past, so it works for the walk to the lighthouse and for the swim across the bay: We would walk to the lighthouse after dinner. The village boys would swim across the bay in August. Being afraid of the sea and hating car journeys are states, not repeated actions: "Nabil would be afraid of the open sea" and "Mona would hate long car journeys" are both wrong, and only "used to" can carry a past state.

questions.prompt: One verb breaks the parallel structure of this sentence. Which part is wrong? "In the past, families used to ① spend the summer on the farm, ② helped with the harvest, ③ pick olives in autumn and ④ tell stories at night."

options.text: ① spend the summer on the farm
② helped with the harvest
③ pick olives in autumn
④ tell stories at night

questions.explanation: After "used to", every verb of the list must keep the same base form, so "helped with the harvest" breaks the series and should read "help with the harvest". Repeating one and the same form, tense or structure right through a sentence is what we call parallelism, and the three other parts — spend, pick and tell — already share it. The break almost always hides in a list, which is why you should read a list back from its end.

questions.prompt: Nizar wants to ask a friend whether collecting stamps was one of his childhood habits. Which question is correct English?

options.text: Did you use to collect stamps?
Did you use to collecting stamps?
Did you used to collect stamps?
Do you used to collect stamps?

questions.explanation: In a question the helper "did" carries the past, so "used" goes back to "use" and the main verb keeps its base form: Did you use to collect stamps? The classic mistake is "Did you used to collect stamps?", which marks the past twice. "Do you used to collect stamps?" mixes a present helper with a past form, and "Did you use to collecting stamps?" puts an -ing form where the base form belongs.

questions.prompt: Complete: "We spent every August by the sea. Then, in 2015, my parents ___ a small house in the mountains and everything changed."

options.text: used to buy
were buying
would buy
bought

questions.explanation: "In 2015" points to one finished event on a named date, and a single completed action of the past takes the past simple: my parents bought a small house. "used to buy" and "would buy" both announce an action that came back many times, which buying a house in one named year is not, and "were buying" would describe an action in progress around another one. Habit structures and the past simple do not compete: they answer different questions.

questions.prompt: You are writing the comparison paragraph "Holidays in the past and holidays today". Which sentence links the two periods correctly?

options.text: Unlike people used to holiday with relatives, today they travel with friends.
People used to holiday with relatives, however today they travel with friends.
People used to holiday with relatives; today, in contrast, they travel with friends.
People used to holiday with relatives, in contrast they now travel with their friends.

questions.explanation: "In contrast" cannot glue two clauses with a simple comma: it needs a full stop or a semicolon before it, and it sits between commas — People used to holiday with relatives; today, in contrast, they travel with friends. Putting "however" after a comma repeats exactly the same mistake, and "unlike" must be followed by a noun or a pronoun, as in Unlike their parents, young people travel with friends, never by a whole clause.

questions.prompt: Two groups ranked the same five outings. Children: the seaside 1 · the zoo 2 · a picnic 3 · a country walk 4 · a museum 5. Adults: the seaside 1 · a country walk 2 · a picnic 3= · a museum 3= · the zoo 5. Which statement do the two columns support?

options.text: Children and adults agree on the picnic only.
The country walk climbs two places for adults.
The museum comes last in both of the two rankings.
The zoo is the adults' second choice.

questions.explanation: The country walk is fourth for the children and second for the adults, so it climbs two places — the only statement the two columns support. The groups also agree on the seaside, which they both put first, so the picnic is not their only meeting point; the zoo is what the children ranked second, not the adults; and the museum comes last for the children but shares third place with the picnic among the adults, as the mark "3=" shows.
